caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 65 of 1986.
lawyer:
Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed, Mohammadullah, Giasuddin Ahmed and Mohd. Ismail Gazi, Advocates  ----- For the Appellant. 
Dr. Rafiqur Rahman, Ruhul Amin and Sirajur Rahman, Advocates ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Progati Industries Ltd ----- Appellant
Vs.
Shahida Khatun and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque J: This appeal at the instance of the defendant No. 1 appellant M/s. Progati Industries Ltd is directed against the judgment dated 15.7.86 and decree dated 21.7.86 passed by Mr. Nurun Nabi Chowdhury, the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court Dhaka In Title Suit No. 347 of 1977.

2. Deceased plaintiff Abdul Halim who died during the pendency of the suit filed Title Suit No. 347 of 1977 in the First Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka on 14.9.1977 against defendants for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession in the suit property measuring 1.50 acres of land with buildings and structures thereon appertaining to plot  Nos. 151 and 157 of Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka.

3. The case of the plaintiff, inter alia, was that he acquired the suit land from the then Government of East Bengal by lease deed executed on 25.1.56 and registered on 22.3.56; that after getting possession therein the plaintiff, as proprietor of Dhaka Wood Works constructed a workshop there and carried on his business; that subsequently the plaintiff, his son Abdul Kader and wife Shahida Khatun formed and incorporated in September, 1959 a private limited company under the name of M/s. Dacca Wood Works Ltd; that the said company obtained loan of Tk. 1,50,000.00 from the Pakistan Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation hereinafter referred to as the PICIC by mortgaging the suit property; that on the failure of the said company to repay the said loan with interest PICIC filed Title Suit No. 315 of 1968 in the 1st Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for realisation of Taka 1,64,952.23 by selling the properties of the plaintiff including the suit land; that the said suit was ultimately decreed on compromise; that in terms of the compromise petition the plaintiff was to pay the sum of Rs. 90,667/00 in two equal installments; the first installment fell due on 31st December 1970 and the second installment fell due on 31st December 1971; that the plaintiff paid the 1st installment on 12.3.70 but could not pay the 2nd installment due to war of liberation though he was ready to pay the 2nd installment within the stipulated time for which no action was taken by the decree-holder; that the plaintiff being managing director of the said company entered into an agreement on 29.11.1969 with M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipment’s Ltd to transfer the suit property but ultimately the said agreement fell through and no further transaction took place and the plaintiff remained absolute owner of the suit property; that after liberation of Bangladesh the defendant No. 1, M/s. Progati Industries Ltd. illegally and forcibly took possession of the suit property in March 1972 by dispossessing the plaintiff; that the defendants have no right, title and interest to possess the same denying title of the plaintiff necessitating declaration of plaintiffs title in the suit property.

4. The defendants No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying material allegations in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that the suit was bad for defect of parties; that the suit was not Maintainable; that the plaintiff has no title and possession in the suit property; that the story of dispossession of the plaintiff by the defendant No. 1 in March 1972 is false; that the plaintiff had no cause of action for the suit against the defendant No. 1 and liable to be dismissed for want of cause of action, that the plaintiff intentionally made false and misstatement regarding the terms of compromise; that the plaintiff did not pay 1st installment or any money under the decree on 12.3.70 or any other date; that it is not true that the agreement with M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipment’s Ltd. hereinafter referred to as the purchaser company fell through and the plaintiff remained absolute owner of the suit property; that the plaintiff has intentionally suppressed material facts; that suit property was mortgaged to the PICIC who filed Title suit No. 315/1968 against the plaintiff and others and the said purchaser company who was in possession of the said properties was added as defendant No. 5; that the said suit was decreed on compromise for a sum of Tk. 90,667.00 and on payment of the same the suit properties was to be redeemed in favour of the added defendant and all the documents of the suit property was to be returned to the added defendant, the said purchaser company; that in terms of the decree the purchaser company made part payment and after liberation the said purchaser company vested in the Government of Bangladesh as abandoned property end at that time the sum of Tk. 50,947.64 was due to Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha; that thereafter ownership of the properties together with all assets and liabilities of the said purchaser company merged with and vested in M/s. Progati Industries Ltd. by virtue of Government Order dated 16.9.72 and 18.10.72; that the defendant No. 1 paid off the decrectal dues of the Title Suit No. 315 of 1968 and received full payment and clearance certificate from Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha; hereinafter referred to as the BSRS, that the defendant No. 1 after taking over and merger of the said purchaser company and payment of all the dues under the decree became exclusive owner of the properties and business in question and neither the plaintiff nor M/s. Dacca Wood Works Ltd has any interest or possession in the same; that the purchaser company developed and renovated the factory at a cost of Tk. 2,00,000.00 during 1968-70 and defendant No. 1 at a cost of Tk. 3,00,000.00 in 1973-75; that the purchaser company was in possession and plaintiff was not in possession and interest and possession of the purchaser company in the suit property vested in the Government after liberation and deft No. 1 got possession from the Government by filing an additional written statement the defendant No. 1 stated, inter alia, that the plaintiff to pay the mortgage dues of the PICIC during pendency of TS 315 of 1968 with permission of the PICIC entered into an agreement on 29.2.69 with the purchaser company to sell the suit property at Tk. 3,60,000.00 and agreed to pay Tk. 1,36,000.00 to the PICIC and Tk. 2,24,000.00 to the plaintiff and in part performance of the said contract possession of the suit property was delivered to purchaser company who was added as defendant No. 5 in that suit; that the purchaser company paid Tk. 45,333.00 to the PICIC on 12,3,1970 and total sum of Taka 1,25,793.51 to the plaintiff in several on compromise on 18.11.70 and in terms of the said decree the purchaser company furnished bank guarantee of Taka 90,667.00 to pay the decretal dues in two installments of Tk. 45,333.00 on 31.12.70 and Tk. 45,334.00 on 31.12.71 and in terms of the compromise decree on payment of the said installments the mortgaged suit property would be redeemed in favour of the added defendant (purchaser company) and the documents relating to the said property would be returned to the said added defendant by the mortgagee and right of redemption was abandoned by the plaintiff; that after passing of the said decree the purchaser company paid the sum of Taka 45,333/00 to PICIC on 31.12.70 and Taka 97,903/59 in kind to the plaintiff who acknowledged the same by granting a receipt on 15.7.71 and Tk. 3021/90 remained due; that the last installment of Tk. 45,334.00 payable to the PICIC could not be paid on the date fixed owing to the changed conditions arising in the country and the same with interest was paid to BSRS which granted necessary clearance certificate and by virtue of the said payment the mortgaged property was fully redeemed in favour of the Government of Bangladesh and plaintiff filed the suit suppressing the material facts; that the purchaser company vested in the Government of Bangladesh as abandoned property having been put into possession of the suit properties in part performance of the written contract for sale dated 29.11.1969 the plaintiff is debarred under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act from enforcing any right in respect of the suit properties in possession of the defendants and plaintiff's suit is liable to be dismissed. Upon the aforesaid pleadings following issues were framed:

1. Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

2. Have the plaintiffs right, title and interest in the suit property and are the plaintiffs entitled to a decree for a declaration of title in respect of the same?

3. Arc the plaintiffs entitled to a decree for recovery of khas possession of the suit property?

4. To what relief, if any, are the plaintiffs entitled?

5. The substituted plaintiffs in support of their case examined 3 witnesses including plaintiff No. 1 (c) and proved documents marked Exts. 1 to 4 and the defendants and produced documents marked Ext. A to Z(7).

6. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record decreed the suit holding that (1) that the suit is maintainable (2) that Title Suit No. 315/1968 filed by the PICIC was decreed on compromise on 18.11.70(3) that the plaintiff entered into an agreement on 29.11.69 with M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipment’s Ltd. to sell the suit property but no possession as per the said agreement was delivered to the said purchaser and the plaintiff was in possession of the Suit property till his dispossession by defendant No. 1 in 1972; (4) that the deceased plaintiff was the absolute owner of the suit property and the defendant No. 1 admitted the ownership and title of the plaintiff in paragraph 7 of the written statement (5) that installments were not paid by M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipment’s Ltd according to the terms of the compromise decree and unless a final decree was passed ownership of the mortgagor was not extinguished and still subsists (6) that the Government did not take over the control and management of the suit property by notification and as such suit properties do not come within the purview of Acting President's Order No. 1/1972 and the suit property is not an abandoned property (7) that since the defendant No. 1 dispossessed the plaintiffs, they are entitled to recover khas possession from the trespasser.

7. Mr. Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed, learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the agreement dated 29.11.1969 between the deceased plaintiff and M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd. marked Ext. 4 was acted upon inasmuch as the purchaser company' was added as defendant No. 5 in the Title Suit No. 315/1968 filed by the PICIC against the plaintiff and others and the plaintiff entered into the said agreement with permission of the PICIC and the said purchaser company agreed to pay the entire mortgage debt of the plaintiff to the PICIC in terms of the compromise decree marked Ext. 3 and the said purchaser company not only paid the dues of the PICIC in terms of the said decree and also paid the amounts due to the deceased plaintiff in terms of the said agreement and referred to the documents marked Exts A, Compromise decree, Ext. B receipt dt.12.3.70 for Rs. 45. 333/00, Ext. B (1) dt. 28.12.70 letter regarding payment of Rs. 45, 333/00 by pay order and Ext B(II) letter dated 9.1.71 about the said payment to PICIC Ext C receipt dt. 29.11.69 fox Rs. 65,000/00, Ext. D receipt dt. 16.12.69 for Rs. 25,793/51 Ext. E receipt dt. 17.12.69 for Rs. 25,000/- Ext. 'F' receipt dt. 2.10.70 for Rs. 10,000/00 Ext. 'G' acknowledgment dt. 15.7.71 for Rs. 97,903.59 all granted by the deceased plaintiff Abdul Halim in terms of the agreement for sale Ext. 'H' receipt dt. 15.9.73 for Taka 50,047/67 b3 the BSRS, the successor of PICIC in satisfaction of the last instalment of Rs. 45,334/00 due on 31.1.71 with interest and Ext. 1(II) clearance certificate dt 15.12.73 by the BSRS. He further submitted that it terms of the said compromise decree payment of the amounts under the decree by the said purchase' company to the PICIC the mortgaged suit prowl; was to be redeemed in favour of the said purchase company and all documents of title relating to the said property was to be returned to the said purchase company and in default of such payment if till mortgaged property were to be put to the sale ant after satisfaction of the dues of the PICIC balance was to be refunded to the said purchaser company and thus the plaintiff relinquished all his interest b the suit property under the said decree which also confirmed the earlier agreement for sale date 29.11.69. He further submitted that in view of the admission of delivery of possession in paragraph No. 5 of the said agreement produced and proved by the plaintiff as Ext. 4 oral evidence to the contrary by the PWs was neither admissible nor could be relied on more so in view of the evidence of possession by the PWs. He further submitted that the suit was bad for defect of parties for not impleading M/S. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd. Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha, Bangladesh, Steel and Engineering Corporation, the controlling Corporation, of the defendant No. 1 M/s. Progati Industries Ltd and for the Government of Bangladesh not being represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Commerce instead of the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, who had nothing to do with the abandoned firms and companies. He further submitted that Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 was amendment by PO 151 of 1972 delating the provision regarding publication in the Gazettee notification with effect from 3.1.72 for taking over management of any abandoned firm or company and as such the decision of the Government dt. 31.1.72 marked Ext. 'M' and letter of appointment dated 15.2.72 marked Ext. appointing DW 1 M Mazammel Huq as Administrator of the said purchaser company treated as abandoned company should have been relied on to hold that all the rights and interests and possession of the purchaser company in the suit property under the said agreement dated 29.11.69 vested in the Government as abandoned property inasmuch as admissibility of the same was not challenged at the time of proving the same by the DW 1 who was competent to prove the same and there was no necessity of mentioning the said letters in the written statement when the fact about said purchaser company being vested as abandoned property in the Government was clearly mentioned in the written statement of the defendant No. 1. He further submitted that in terms of the said agreement for sale dated 29.11.69 and compromise decree dated 18.11.70 the plaintiff was not entitled to declaration of title and recovery of possession in the suit property such suit was barred under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act as the purchaser company was in possession in part let formance of the said written contract for sale and the said interest and possession having been vested in the Government as abandoned property now managed by the defendant No. 1 M/s. Progati Industries Ltd. after its taking over and merger with the purchaser company vide Government decision dated 10.9.72 marked Ext 'O' and decision dated 16.10.72 marked Ext. 'P' and Gazettee Notification dated 18.5.72 marked Ext. R(1) and dated 7.7.72 marked Ext R. He further submitted that plaintiffs have totally failed to prove possession and dispossession in the st. it property and trial Court erred in decreeing the suit which was liable to be dismissed as the same was barred by limitation.

8. Mr. Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff respondents, submitted that the suit as framed for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession of the suit land against the trespasser M/s. Progati Industries Ltd was not bad for defect of parties inasmuch as the said trespasser and the Government of Bangladesh under the provision of PO 142 of 1972 were the only necessary parties. He further submitted that the deceased plaintiff was admittedly in possession of the suit property upto 29.11.69 when the deed of agreement for sale of the suit property was executed and if time is calculated from that date then the suit was filed within 12 years on 14.9.77 and the suit was not barred by limitation. But the learned counsel found it difficult to support the judgment in the face of the pleadings and the evidence on record.

<u>9. We have been led through the pleadings, oral and documentary evidence on record and also the impugned judgment in this appeal. We have considered the arguments from both sides with reference to the pleadings evidence on record and the impugned judgment and decree. We have noticed that the issues were re-cast by the trial Court on 28.6.86 in course of hearing arguments in the suit. No issue regarding defect of parties or limitation was framed by the Trial Court after recasting the issues. The defendant No. 1 in paras 4 and 12 of their written statement raised the question of defect of parties but there is no pleading regarding the suit being barred by limitation. From the pleadings and evidence on record we find that the suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession having been filed on 16.9.77 from the alleged date of dispossession in March 1972 was apparently not barred by limitation under Article 142 of the Limitation Act and that is why bar of Limitation was not pleaded by the defendant. The defendant No. 1 is a nationalised company placed under the Bangladesh Engineering and Ship Building Corporation as per Gazettee notification dated 18.3.72 Ext. R(1) and Gazettee notification dated 7.7.72 Ext: R correcting the earlier notification. The said corporation was subsequently renamed as the Bangladesh Steel and Engineering Corporation. The defendant No. 1 has not lost its legal entity as a juristic person and can sue and be said without the said corporation which controls and supervises its activities under the provisions of Bangladesh Industrial Enterprises (Nationalisation) Order 1972 (P 0 No. 27 of 1972) and as such the suit could proceed against the defendant No. 1 without impleading the said corporation. Under the provision of Section 6 of the Bangladesh Transfer of Immovable Property (Temporary Provision;) Order 1972 (PO 142 of 1972) the Government is a necessary party in a suit for declaration of title when directly or indirectly Government is going to be affected and under the provision of section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure "Government is to be represented either by the Deputy Commissioner or by the Secretary of the Government when affairs of the Railways is not involved in the suit. The defendant No. 1 in their written statement has not specifically raised any objection as to the Government defendant No. 2 not being represented by the Secretary of the appropriate Ministry instead of the Deputy Commissioner and as such we are of the view that the suit was not bad for defect of the parties. In this appeal we are to see whether the learned trial Court was justified in holding that the plaintiff had title and possession till he was dispossessed by the defendant No. 1. Admittedly the deceased plaintiff became owner and possessor of the suit property as per deed of agreement for lease dated 25.1.1956 Ext. 1 on payment of Rs. 3,375/- as part of the premium out of total premium of Rs. 27,675/- undertaking to pay the balance Rs. 24,300/- in twenty equal annual instalments and annual rent of Rs. 450/- to the Government. Admittedly the deceased plaintiff entered into written agreement on 29.11.1969 Ext. 4 to sell the suit property to the purchaser company at a consideration of Rs. 3,60,000/- on receipt of Rs. 65,000/- as advance as acknowledged in paragraph 4 of the said agreement as well as by granting a separate receipt dated 29.11.69 Ext. C for Rs. 65,000/00 by two cheques. Delivery of vacant physical possession of the demised suit property to the said purchaser company was as know lodged in paragraph No. 5 of the said agreement. We find from the said agreement that the deceased plaintiff entered into the said agreement to raise money to pay mortgage debt of his M/s. Dacca Wood Works Ltd to the PICIC and the purchaser company agreed to furnish a bank guarantee for Rs. 1,36,000/- in favour of the PICIC who shall redeem the suit mortgage property in favour of the said purchaser company on receipt of the said Bank guarantee and on completion of all the instalments of the Bank guarantee property shall automatically be redeemed in favour of the said purchaser company and all documents shall be returned to the said purchaser company by the PICIC who will also withdraw TS No. 315/1968 from the 1st court of Sub-Judge, Dhaka and that further sum of Rs. 50,000/00 shall be paid by 15th December 1969 and balance sum of Rs 1,09,000/00 will be paid at the time of registration of the sale deed. From the compromise decree dated 18.11.1970 Ext. 3 as well as Ext. "A we find that the said Title Suit was filed on 19.11.68 by the PICIC against M/s. Dacca Wood Works Ltd, deceased plaintiff and other directors of the said company for enforcement of mortgage by deposit of title deeds for realization of Rs. 1,69,952/23 by sale of the mortgaged property and the said purchaser company was added as defendant No. 5 on 12.6.70 and the deceased plaintiff entered into the said agreement on 29.11.89 with the said purchaser company with the permission of the PICIC on condition .of furnishing a bank guarantee for Rs. 1,36,000/- to PICIC in full and final settlement of the loan of M/s. Dacca Wood Works Ltd and that the PICIC received the sum of Tk. 45,333/00 by a pay order dated 12.3.70 from the said purchaser company and encased the same on 2.4.70 and the said purchaser company also furnished a Bank guarantees for Rs. 90,667/00 in favour of the PICIC guaranteeing payment of Rs. 45,333/00 on 31.12.70 and Rs. 45,334/00 on 31.12.71; that on such payments being made the mortgaged suit property shall be redeemed in favour of the said purchaser company and the documents relating to the said properties shall be returned to the said purchaser company but in default of payment of the said instalments the mortgaged suit property shall be sold and the money thus realised shall be applied in payment of the amounts due to the PICIC and balance amount, if any, shall be paid to the said purchaser company.</u>

<u>Now we are to see how far the said purchaser company fulfilled the terms of the said agreement Ext. 4 with the deceased plaintiff and terms of the said decree Ext. 3 with the PICIC.</u>

10. DW 1 Md. Mozammel Huq in his deposition proved Ext. 'C' dated 29.11.69, a receipt for Rs. 65,000/00, Ext. 'E' dated 16.12.69, another receipt for Rs. 25,793/51, Ext. 'E' dated 17.12.69, another receipt for Rs. 25,000/00 Ext. 'F' dated 2.10.70, another receipt for Rs. 10,000/00 and Ext.'G' dated 15.7.91, an acknowledgment of Rs. 97,903/59 in the form of spare parts etc all granted by the deceased plaintiff. Most of these documents marked as exhibits with objection though the same were formally proved by the DW 1. The plaintiffs challenged the said documents mainly on the ground that the signatures of the deceased plaintiff appearing in these receipts were not those of the deceased plaintiff. On comparison of the signatures of the deceased plaintiff appearing in the plaint with the signatures appearing in the said receipts we are satisfied that those arc in the same hand. Thus we find that the said purchaser company paid the sum of Rs. 2,23,697/10 to the deceased plaintiff out of total Rs. 2,24,000/00 payable to him 'by the purchaser company under the said agreement. DWI also proved Ext. B dated 12.3.70 for Rs. 45,333/00 Ext. B (1) dated 28.12.70 and B(II) dated 9.1.71 towards payment of Rs. 45,333/00 paid to the PICIC and Ext. H dated 15.9.73 for Taka 50,947/67 paid to BSRS successor of the PICIC with interest. Ext. 1 (2) dated 15.12.73 is a clearance certificate issued by the BSRS in favour of the M/s. Progati Industries Ltd who paid the said sum of Taka 50,947/67 claiming to be successor of the purchaser company. On consideration of the said documents we find that the purchaser company and after liberation the defendant paid all the dues of the PICIC and BSRS payable under said the decree. The court below failed to notice that by Ext. 'B' dated Rs. 45,333/00 was paid by the purchaser company and the same is also acknowledged in para 5 of the compromise petition and it was wholly wrong to hold that the purchaser company did not pay the same. Moreover the court below failed to consider Ext. B (1) dated 28.12.70 and Ext. B(II) dated 9.1.71 toward payment of Rs. 45,333/00 in satisfaction of the 1st instalment due on 31.12.70 and thus the court below was not fully correct to find that the purchaser company could not pay the decretal instalment within the stipulated time. It is true that the last instalment due on 31.12.71 could not be paid in time though covered by the bank guarantee. But after liberation the defendant No. 1 paid the last instalment with interest. But the court below termed the said payment as unauthorised on an erroneous view that right of redemption under the deed could not be exercised by any person other than the purchaser company without noticing and considering F series by which BSRS as the successor of PICIC released and discharged the defendant No. 1 from the obligation contained in the documents executed by M/s. Dacca Wood Works Ltd. and Bank guarantee furnished by the purchaser company in respect of the said loan. Neither PICIC nor its successor BSRS ever attempted to sell the suit mortgaged property in exercise of the right under the said decree and the said decree-holder is not a party in this suit and there is no question of redemption or sale of the suit property under the said decree in this suit and thus the court below misdirected itself to hold that the right of the original mortgagor still subsists and not extinguished since no final decree has been passed.

11. Admittedly the purchaser company purchased the suit property in terms of the said agreement from the deceased plaintiff admitting his leasehold title therein and no sale deed has yet been executed and registered in favour of the purchaser company though almost entire consideration had been paid to the deceased plaintiff in terms of the said agreement.

12. The plaintiff did not challenge the validity of the said agreement in the plaint except alleging in paragraph No. 8 of the plaint that the said agreement fell through and no further transaction had taken place without even alleging that possession was not delivered to the purchaser but we have already found that the deceased plaintiff received almost the entire consideration and a sum of Taka 302/90 is due from the purchaser company. Moreover we have also found that the said agreement was acted upon in terms of payment of the dues of the PICIC and its successor BSRS under the said decree Ext. 3 and payments to the deceased plaintiff. PW 1 who is substituted plaintiff No.1 (c) in his deposition as PW 1 stated that his father received Tk. 65,000/00 from the purchaser company under the said agreement dated 29.11.69 proved by him as Ext. 4 but the purchaser company did not perform their part of the contract nor paid the consideration money and thus the agreement became unenforceable and ceased to exist and delivery of possession was never given to the purchaser company and in March 1972 the defendant No. 1 dispossessed them from the suit land. He admitted in cross-examination that contents of the agreement Ext. 4 was correctly written. He did not remember the date of dispossession and did not lodge any complaint against such dispossession. He did not know the holding number of contiguous boundary plots. PW 2 who claimed to be a polish mistry stated that in March 1972 some unknown persons putting on khaki dress dispossessed them from the suit land. In cross-examination he stated that he did not know the holding number of the neighboring plots. There were five miseries including him and many other persons gathered there at the time of dispossession. He had no paper to show that he was polish mistry at the time. PW 3 who also claimed to be another polish mistry stated that in March 1972 some persons along with some khaki dressed men forcibly dispossessed them from the suit land. In cross examination he stated that he did not know the holding numbers of the neighbouring houses. There were no other persons except polish mistries at the time of dispossession. Though such oral evidence contrary to the pleadings and terms of the said written agreement regarding delivery of possession to the purchaser company was not admissible in evidence under the provision of section 92 of the Evidence Act, the court below considered such evidence along with address of M/s. Dacca Wood Works Ltd. at 151 & 152 Tejgaon Industrial Area in the printed pads on which Exts. CDE and F were typed written and alleged failure of defendant No. 1 to produce any paper to show that the purchaser company (M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd.) was in possession of the suit property and also address of the said company in the order dated 12.6.70 of Ext. 3 at 12/13 Motijheel Commercial Area to hold that possession of the suit property was not delivered to purchaser company as per agreement Ext. 4 and that the deceased plaintiff was in possession of the same till he was dispossessed by the defendant No. 1 in 1972. We find from letter dated 15.7.1971 written by the deceased plaintiff to the Managing Director of the purchaser company marked Ext. "G" that office of Dacca Wood Works Ltd. was at 44-45 North Brook Hall Road and that of the purchaser company was at 151-152 Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka. Similarly from letter dated 17.3.70 written by the deceased plaintiff to the Manager of the purchaser company marked Ext. K we find that there is an admission that assembly plant of the purchaser company was at Tejgaon in the premises purchased from him where the purchaser company was shifting their office from Motijheel and he had prayed to appoint him as the selling agent in the present office of the purchaser company. From appointment letter dated 15.2.1972 written by the Chairman and Member Secretary of the Management Board 'F' appointing DW 1 Md. Mozammel Huq sales-in-charge of the purchaser company as administrator of the purchaser company Ext. N. We find that office of the purchaser company was at 151-152 Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka. DW 1 stated that he was sales-in-charge of M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Lts. in 1968 and in his presence on 22.11.69 Abdul Halim entered into the contract for sale of the suit property to M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd. and the said Vendor delivered possession of the suit premises to M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd. on the date on receipt of Rs. 65,000/- and the suit property was in possession of the purchaser company from 29.11.69 and after liberation the Government took over possession of the same as abandoned property and since 16.11.72 M/s. Progati Industries Ltd. was in possession and since 29.11.69 neither Abdul Halim now Dacca Wood Works Ltd. had any possession in the suit property. In cross examination he could not be shaken. DW 2 stated that he was security guard of the M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd. and he knew the plaintiff who delivered possession of the suit property on 29.11.69 to M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd. and the said company was in possession and subsequently defendant No. 1 had been in possession. In cross examination he also could not be shaken and denied the suggestion that defendant No. 1 forcibly took possession of the suit land in March, 1972. PW 1 is an interested witness so also the other PWs who have no knowledge of the suit property. No trustworthy and independent witness from the neighbouring houses could be produced by the plaintiffs. Their evidence contrary to the pleadings and terms of the agreement Ext. 4 which is admittedly correctly written is not admissible and are not also trustworthy and can not be relied on. On the other hard, evidence of the DWs discussed above though they were employees of the purchaser company appears to be competent and trustworthy. The court below wrongly relied on the address of Dacca Wood Works Ltd. in the old printed pads retained by the deceased plaintiff and address of the purchaser company in the order dated 12.6.70 of Ext. 3 to come to an erroneous decision that possession was not delivered to the purchaser company.

13. In consideration of the evidence discussed above we have no hesitation to hold that possession of the suit property was delivered by the deceased plaintiff Abdul Halim on 29.11.69 to the purchaser company (M/s. Rana Tractor and Equipments Ltd.) in part performance of the contract for sale Ext. 4 and since then the said purchaser company was in possession of the suit property and the deceased plaintiff had no possession in the suit property since 29.11.69 and the deceased plaintiff was not dispossessed from the suit property by defendant No. 1 in March 1972.

14. The defendant No. 1 is admittedly in possession of the suit land. Now we are to see how the defendant No. 1 has been possessing the suit land and whether the defendant No. 1 is liable to be ejected and the plaintiff is entitled to recover possession from the defendant No. 1. The defendant No. 1, Progati Industries Ltd. is a nationalized company and claimed that the purchaser company (M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd) was an abandoned property and all its assets and liabilities merged with the defendant No. 1. DW 1 stated "the registered office of M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd was at Lahore. The Directors were Pakistanis who resided at Lahore. After liberation of Bangladesh all its properties including the disputed properties vested in the Government as abandoned property under PO No. 16 of 1972. The Government formed a Board to control and manage the abandoned properties by order No. IV-142 dated 31.1.72 marked Ext. M. The Management Board (Group F) appointed me, Md. Mozammel Hoque as Administrator. This is the order of appointment being CIE/DA/Management Board-F/1/72/A-1224 dated 15.2 72 marked Ext. N According to this order of appointment run the management up to 15.11.72 and since 16.11.72 as per order of the Government M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd was merged with Progati Industries Ltd. This is the letter dated 16.9.72 written by Section Officer, Ministry of Commerce to Progati Industries Ltd for absorption marked Ext. 'O'. By leiter dated 18.10. 72 the Government informed the Administrator of Rana Tractor and Equipments Ltd that Government decided that M/s. Progati Industries Ltd. should accept all assets and liabilities of M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd including staff liabilities. This letter dated 18.10.72 marked Ext. 'P' and by virtue of this letter Rana Tractors and Equipment Ltd was merged with Progati Industries Ltd. On 25.1.73 we submitted an audit report upto 15th November, 1972. This is the letter dated 25.1.73 along with audit report marked Ext. 'Q' and the audit report is marked Ext. Q(1)". The plaintiffs did not challenge the said evidence in cross examination and no objection as to admissibility of the said documents were noted in the deposition sheet nor in the list of exhibited documents. The court below observed: "That the admissibility of Ext. LMN were challenged by the plaintiffs saying that those documents cannot be taken into consideration inasmuch as the defendant has not made any averment in the written statement about those documents. Moreover Ext. L and N do not show that Dacca Wood Works Ltd or its properties was declared abandoned property by the Government. The said exhibits do not contain the suit properties. The said Ext. N cannot be taken in to consideration and the same was not proved by its author and does not also show that the suit property was declared as abandoned property. The owners of Dacca Wood Works Ltd are nationals of Bangladesh and the Government did not take over the control and management of the suit property by notification and as such suit property does not come within the purview of Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972. The suit property is not an abandoned property. The defendant No. 1 stated in paras 13 and 14 of the written statement that after liberation of Bangladesh M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd. vested In the Government of Bangladesh as abandoned property and thereafter ownership of the properties together with assets and liabilities of M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd was vested in Progati Industries Ltd by virtue of Government orders dated 16.9.72 and 18.10.72. In our view the aforesaid pleading was very clear and sufficient to understand the defence case and there was no requirement of law at the time of filing the written statement on 3.7.1978 by defendant No. 1 to produce in court along with the written statement the documents in its possession upon which it relied and also to furnish list of other documents not in its possession upon which it relied. Aforesaid provision was made by amending Order VIII rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure by Ordinance No. LVIII of 1983 and it was not retrospective in operation and no procedural law could have retrospective operation. We are therefore of the view the court below was not justified in not considering the said documents produced and proved by the DW 1 who was competent to prove the same being the officer incharge of the said purchaser company since before liberation and immediately after liberation on 15.2.72 he was appointed Administrator by the Government treating the said purchaser company as abandoned under the Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972. The provision for taking over an abandoned firm by Gazettee Notification was deleted with effect from 3.1.72 the date of promulgating APO No. 1/72 by PO No. 151 of 1972. In consideration of the aforesaid evidence on record we hold that M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd vested in the Government of Bangladesh as abandoned property and Government appointed DW 1 as Administrator of the same on 15.2.72 and thereafter all its assets and liabilities were taken over and merged with the defendant No. 1 with effect from 16.11.72 and the defendant No. 1 was not in possession of the suit property in March, 1972 when the plaintiff was allegedly dispossessed. We further find from the audit report of M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd. upto 15.11.72 Ext. '0(1) that the said purchaser company bought land and buildings at a cost of Taka 3,60,000.00 and the same was shown as asset of the said company. This asset is nothing but the interest of the said purchaser company under the deed of agreement dated 29.11.69 Ext 4 to purchase the suit property in which the purchaser company got delivery of possession in part performance of the said contract and the purchaser company continued in possession till liberation of Bangladesh and after liberation the DW 1 continued in possession on behalf of the Government as abandoned property till its absorption on 16.11.72 with the defendant No. 1. We have already found that the deceased plaintiff had no possession in the suit property since 29.11.69 and he was not dispossessed by the defendant No. 1 in March 1972.

15. The defendant No. 1 in its additional written statement set up the defence under section 53 A of the Transfer of Property Act stating that the plaintiff as transferer is debarred from enforcing any right in respect of the suit property in possession of the defendants. Section 53A is as follows :

"53A. Where any person contracts to transfer for consideration any immovable property by writing signed by him or on his behalf from which the terms necessary to constitute the transfer can be ascertained with reasonable certainty, and the transferee has, in part performance of the contract, mess possession of the property or any part thereof, or the transferee being already in possession continues in possession in part performance of the contract and has done some act in furtherance of the contract,

and the transferee has performed or is willing to perform his part of the contract.

then, notwithstanding that the contract though required to be registered, has not been registered, or, where there is an instrument of transfer, that the transfer has not been completed in the manner prescribed therefor by the law for the time being in force, the transferor or any person claiming under him shall be debarred from enforcing against the transferee and persons claiming under him any right in respect of the property of which the transferee has taken or continued in possession, other than a right expressly provided by the terms of the contract:

Provided that nothing in this section shall affect the rights of a transferee for consideration who has no notice of the contract or of the pail performance thereof."

16. We also find from evidence of the DW 1 that M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd. was always ready and willing to perform their part of the contract and they paid almost the entire consideration money leaving the balance of Taka 302.90. Letter dated 3.11.71 Ext. J written by M/s. Rana Tractor and Equipments Ltd. to deceased plaintiff Abdul Halim shows that he was requested to give no objection' certificate to enable them to get the sale deed registered in their name as early as possible. Thus it is clear that the said purchaser company had performed almost the entire part of their obligation under the contract and has always been ready and willing to perform their remaining part of the contract. We have also found that the defendants have been claiming to possess the suit property under the said purchaser company as the interest of the said purchaser in the suit property vested in the defendant No. 2 as abandoned property and under order of the defendant No. 2 assets and liabilities of the purchaser company was taken over and merged with the defendant No. 1.

<u>17. In the case of Abdul Gani Vs. Dina Bandhu reported in 14 DLR 663 the learned Single Judge of the then Dhaka High Court held as follows:</u>

<u>"The right conferred by this section is available for a defendant to protect his possession. For the purpose of protecting his possession the section operates as a bar to the plaintiff asserting his title. In the facts of the present case, the plaintiff is barred under section 53A from asserting his title and is not entitled to get a declaration that he has his right and title in the disputed properties."</u>

18. In the case of Mst. Ghalam Sakhina Vs. Umar Bakh and another reported in 16 DLR SC 389 the Supreme Court of Pakistan held as follows:

"But section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act makes an exception to this and provides that where a person obtains possession of or continues to remain in possession of a property under a document in writing which, though compulsorily registerable, has not been registered, then neither person transferring the property nor any one claiming under him shall be entitled to enforce against the transferee or any person claiming under him any right in respect of that property."

19. From the provisions of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act and the aforesaid decision it is abundantly clear that when a transferor has delivered possession of his property to the transferee in part performance of a written contract neither the transferor nor anyone claiming under him will be permitted to assert his title to the said property or to recover possession of the same from the transferee or any one claiming under him so long the transferee or person claiming under him has done some act in furtherance of the contract and has performed or is ready and willing to perform his part of the contract.

20. In this case the defendants are not the transferees under the agreement Ext. 4 but they claim to possess the suit property under the transferee M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd. and we have also found that the defendants have been possessing the suit property under the said purchaser company vested in the defendant No. 2 as abandoned property.

<u>21. We, therefore, hold that neither the deceased plaintiff was nor his successors, the substituted plaintiffs are entitled to declaration of title in the suit property and the substituted plaintiffs are debarred from asserting their title or any right in the suit property not only against the transferee M/s. Rana Tractors and Equipments Ltd. but also against the defendants who; have been possessing the same under the said purchaser company. So Court below was not justified in declaring plaintiffs title in the suit property. The deceased plaintiff having delivered possession of the suit property in part performance of written contract for sale was not entitled to recover khas possession by ejecting the defendants who are in lawful possession of the suit property. We have already found that the substituted plaintiffs have failed to prove alleged possession and, dispossession. The deceased plaintiff came before the court with a false case and the substituted plaintiffs adduced false oral evidence contrary to the documentary evidence so the suit is liable to be dismissed.</u>

<u>22. In this appeal we are surprised to notice how a Subordinate Judge can be oblivious of the provision of the Evidence Act and decide a question of fact on the basis of inadmissible oral evidence of no worth at all contrary to admitted documentary evidence on record and can also decide question of fact without consideration of the contents of the relevant documentary evidence on record. The learned Subordinate Judge as the Trial Court was the initial court of the fact and had the jurisdiction to arrive at any finding of fact after due and proper consideration of all the admissible evidence on record and not in the slipshod and injudicious manner in which it was done by him. We hope that the learned Judge will be more careful in future and decide cases on proper and due consideration of evidence on record.</u>

23. In the result the appeal is allowed without cost and the judgment and decree appealed against is set aside and the Title Suit No. 347 of 1977 of the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka is dismissed.
